newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenes to vote in general election on Nov 10.
newsitem.headline: Slovenes to vote in general election on Nov 10.

text.p: Slovenian President Milan Kucan said on Thursday his country's third multi-party general election would take place on November 10, despite calls from the right for a referendum on electoral reform.
"It is in the interest of the state that the political tensions of the pre-election battle end as soon as possible," Kucan told a news conference.
The last general election held in the former Yugoslav republic was in 1992. Under the constitution, the last possible date for a fresh poll was December 8.
Kucan said he had made the decision after talking to the leaders of most political parties currently represented in the 90-seat lower house of parliament.
"Although a consensus with all political parties could not be reached, most favoured this date and their opinion was that the election should take place as soon as possible," he added.
The centrist Liberal Democrats of Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek, currently leading in opinion polls, were known to favour November 10 as the election date.
But the main opposition Social Democrats had urged Kucan to delay the vote until the Constitutional Court had ruled on whether a referendum on electoral reform should be held first.
"I made this decision only after it was clear a referendum could not take place before October 8, which was the deadline for determining the election date," Kucan said.
Parliament voted in August to hold the referendum after the next election but the rightist Social Democrats appealed to the court, which is expected to issue its ruling on September 10.
"A referendum could still take place before the election but it cannot change the rules (of the November 10 poll)," Kucan said.
Some 1.5 million Slovenes are eligible to vote for the 27 political parties expected to contest the election.
Elections for the 30-seat upper house of parliament are due to take place by the end of 1997.
Slovenia, which borders Italy, Austria, Croatia and Hungary, has one of the most successful economies among ex-communist states in central and eastern Europe with a per capita GDP of $9,352 in 1995.
But Drnovsek's government was forced to relax tight monetary control during the election year following a number of protracted strikes in the public sector.

Kucan, a former leading figure in both the Yugoslav and Slovenian communist parties, has been credited with steering the small Alpine nation towards a solid democracy since it declared independence from former Yugoslavia in June 1991.
With nationalist presidents in Croatia and Serbia and potential instability in Bosnia despite this month's elections, a stable Slovenia occupies a strategic position on the edge of the Balkan region.
Slovenia is likely to be included in the first wave of new members to join NATO next year and has made a formal application for membership of the European Union.
